newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: With Bosnian deal done, Holbrooke goes to Belgrade.
newsitem.headline: With Bosnian deal done, Holbrooke goes to Belgrade.

text.p: U.S. envoy Richard Holbrooke ended a row between Bosnia's squabbling leaders over ambassadorial posts on Friday, then promptly headed to Belgrade to lean on Yugoslav President Slobodan Milosevic to fulfil his part of the Dayton accord.
The dispute, which lasted several weeks, had triggered an international freeze on Bosnia's ambassadors.
Under the deal, the Bosnian ambassador to the United Nations will be a Moslem, a Serb will be ambassador to Washington and a Croat will be ambassador to Japan, Holbrooke and other mediators said.
Members of the multi-ethnic collective presidency also agreed on the composition of a joint military commission and on a single area code for Bosnia's telephone network.
"These agreements are full evidence of Western determination (to enforce the peace agreement)," Holbrooke told reporters. "These are steps forward and pretty solid ones."

Diplomats said Holbrooke would now threaten Milosevic with economic sanctions unless he abided by his Dayton commitments, which include handing over indicted war criminal and former Bosnian Serb president Radovan Karadzic and others.
"Holbrooke is bringing a bagful of carrots and sticks. It's up to Milosevic to choose which he would rather have," one said.

As then-president of Serbia, Milosevic was one of the signatories of the Dayton peace accord which Holbrooke helped to engineer and which stipulated that Karadzic, once Milosevic's protege, was to stay out of politics.
A year later, Karadzic and his allies persist in attempting to circumvent the accords and undermine his successor as Bosnian Serb president, Biljana Plavsic.
Plavsic has publicly accused them of plundering the territory Bosnia through vast smuggling rackets and making it their personal fiefdom.
She was thrown out of the Serb ruling party and Karadzic loyalists made moves to impeach her from their mountain resort of Pale.
On his way to Belgrade, Holbrooke flew to the north Bosnian town of Banja Luka to show support for Plavsic.
Calling her a democratically elected, legitimate president, Holbrooke said she was committed "to democracy, and the rule of law and a single Bosnia-Herzegovina with two entities".
"This is the essence of Dayton," he said.
Holbrooke repeated the international community's resolve to see Karadzic handed over to the tribunal on war crimes in former Yugoslavia in The Hague.
The visit was the first time Holbrooke had returned to the Balkans since he forced Karadzic to step down as Bosnian Serb president last year.

The whirlwind trip was a bid by the architect of Dayton to revive the stalling peace process, hampered by bickering among Bosnia's leaders, Karadzic's continued influence and the failure to ensure a safe return for tens of thousands of refugees.

The United States and western European countries had suspended contacts with Bosnian envoys this week after Moslem, Croat and Serb political leaders failed to agree on the allocation of major posts, especially Washington, by an August 1 deadline.
Bosnia's current ambassadors were appointed by the wartime Moslem-led Bosnian government which fought separatist Serbs and, for 10 months, Croat forces, their nominal allies.

As part of the new push for peace, diplomats said they expected the NATO-led SFOR peacekeeping force to announce it would begin supervising local special police forces which are really nothing more than private armies of nationalist leaders.

Milosevic will also face tough questioning about Serbia's handling of human rights in its mostly-Albanian populated province of Kosovo, the freedom of the media in Serbia and the slow pace of democracy and economic reforms.

The diplomats said time and money were running out for the Yugoslav economy as the government struggled hard to maintain order and feed the 11-million strong population, a third of which was living in poverty.
